name: 志な乃
address_ja: 〒103-0004 東京都中央区東日本橋3-1-4
cuisine: Plain old-Tokyo soba-and-udon shop whose signature is the 合盛り — soba and udon laid side by side in one basket with five separate condiments; lunch runs well under ¥2,000
neighborhood: Higashi-Nihonbashi 3-chōme — 3 min from Higashi-Nihombashi (Toei Asakusa line) and Bakuroyokoyama (Toei Shinjuku line), 6 min on foot from Ningyōchō
gf_detail: Not workable, and the house dish makes that unusually plain: the 合盛り is soba and udon served together, so wheat noodles are boiled alongside the buckwheat at every service. The tsuyu is ordinary Edo wheat shōyu. Nothing about allergens, gluten or wheat-free handling appears on any listing for this shop.
vegan_detail: No vegan option is published. Soba/udon tsuyu in a shop of this type is a bonito dashi, and the shop's own well-regarded そばがき is eaten with 生醤油, wasabi, negi and 鰹節. There is no meat-free or fish-free set on any menu that could be found.

roles: owner-operated neighbourhood shop; no chef named in any public source
chef_bio.origin: Higashi-Nihonbashi, Chūō-ku — one of a family of six Tokyo shops trading as 志な乃, all keeping the manner of the parent house in Kannai, Yokohama
chef_bio.background: 志な乃 is not one shop but a small tribe of them: a soba-tasting site that has eaten at every Tokyo branch counts six carrying the name, each following the flow of the original house in Kannai, Yokohama — mingei-style interiors and Mashiko-yaki bowls throughout. The Higashi-Nihonbashi shop is the one nearest Ningyōchō, and the same reviewer singles it out, with the Atago branch, as the best of the six. What sets it apart within the family is the cut: where the other 志な乃 shops serve a broad, rustic 田舎風 noodle, here both soba and udon are cut fine — the soba a deep azuki colour, laid out in neat ranks rather than heaped. The order to place is the 合盛り, soba and udon together, which arrives with five condiments (negi, wasabi, shiso, grated daikon, grated ginger), the convention being negi and wasabi for the soba and the rest for the udon. The udon is what the reviewer rates highest of all. At night the shop also makes そばがき 'kaki-ppanashi', straight from the beating, eaten with raw soy sauce, wasabi, negi and bonito flakes. No chef, owner or founding date is published anywhere; Tabelog carries no phone number and no first-party hours.
chef_bio.specialty: 合盛り (soba and udon in one basket, five condiments); そばがき at night.

anecdotes.text: A soba specialist who has eaten at all six Tokyo 志な乃 shops writes that this one and the Atago branch are the two he would send people to, and that the udon here is 'far, far better' than the Sanuki udon served at Ginza's Sakata.
Unusually for the 志な乃 family, both noodles here are cut fine — the soba nearly as slim as a seiro noodle, deep azuki in colour, and arranged in the basket rather than piled.
A HotPepper user review records simply: 「そばとうどんの合盛がおいしかったです。」

chef_bio.japanese_sources_summary: Tabelog (13008063) gives the name 志な乃, the address 中央区東日本橋3-1-4, coordinates 35.69028/139.78279, cuisine そば・うどん, a 3.60 rating over 106 reviews, hours 月～金 11:15–15:00 and 17:00–20:00 / 土 11:15–14:00, closed Sundays and holidays, and files the shop in the 人形町 area with 「人形町駅、小伝馬町駅より徒歩6分」. cybersoba.com describes the shop in detail and gives the phone number 03-3664-9795. HotPepper carries a live listing at the same address (nearest station 馬喰横山). No page for a shop named 「蕎麦 志乃」 exists on any of them.

gf_cross_contamination.text: The shop's signature dish is soba and udon served together. Wheat noodles go into the same water as the buckwheat at every service — there is no scenario here in which the soba is not exposed to wheat.

soy_sauce_wheat.text: Ordinary wheat shōyu throughout: the tsuyu, and the 生醤油 served with the そばがき. No tamari is mentioned anywhere.

vegan_cross_contact.text: Bonito flakes are served on the そばがき and the tsuyu in a shop of this type is a bonito dashi. No animal-free preparation is published.

cultural_comfort.note: A small, plain shop with no website, no published English, no online booking and — on Tabelog — not even a phone number. Lunchtime is a local office crowd and you order at the table in Japanese. It closes between 15:00 and 17:00 on weekdays, shuts at 14:00 on Saturdays and is closed Sundays and holidays, so check the day before you walk over from Ningyōchō. Say 「合盛り」 and you will get the right thing.

enrich_note: NAME CORRECTION. The light record read 「蕎麦 志乃」 at 人形町駅周辺. Confidence is 'medium' because the identification is an inference from a shared name plus proximity rather than a first-party confirmation, and because six shops share the name — if a human can check, confirm the intended branch before this ships. Note the light record's 'vegan: limited' was inferred from the word 蕎麦 and is unsupported; corrected to 'no'. The original pin (35.685/139.782) was about 600 m south-west of the real address. Also worth flagging: a Yahoo search for 「蕎麦 志乃 人形町」 puts 日本橋 蕎ノ字 (Sonoji, tabelog 13201969) at the top — a ¥30,000+ tempura/soba omakase counter at 日本橋人形町2-22-11. name: とん八亭
cuisine: Fourteen seats, lunch only, one thing done exactly: pork fried in pure lard at 130°C for ten minutes and rested — hire-katsu set ¥2,700, rōsu ¥2,400, bite-size hitokuchi ¥1,800, and the shop closes when the day's pork runs out
neighborhood: Ueno 4-chōme, a block off the Ameyoko arcade — 2 min from JR Okachimachi, 2 min from Ueno-hirokōji (Ginza line) and Ueno-okachimachi (Toei Ōedo), 4 min from Naka-okachimachi (Hibiya), 5 min from Yushima (Chiyoda)
hours_raw: 火～日・祝 11:30～14:00（売り切れ次第終了させて頂きます）　定休日：月曜日 ※祝日の場合は営業して翌日休業 ※他臨時休業あり
gf_detail: A tonkatsu shop is wheat from end to end: flour, egg, panko, and here a single lard fryer that everything passes through — katsu, ebi-fry, oyster fry, croquette. The table sauce is a Japanese Worcester-style sauce (wheat) and the set comes with miso soup. Nothing about allergens or gluten appears on the shop's official gnavi page, its menu page or Tabelog. There is no version of this meal that is safe for a celiac.
vegan_detail: Nothing on the menu is animal-free. Every dish is pork, prawn or oyster, fried in 100% lard; the sets are rice, house pickles and miso soup. Fourteen seats and one fryer means there is no side kitchen to improvise in.

chef_bio.origin: Ueno, Taitō-ku — the shop was founded in 1947 in Ueno-hirokōji's 「たぬき小路」 alley and has stayed in the family since
chef_bio.background: とん八亭 opened in 1947 in the 「たぬき小路」 alley off Ueno-hirokōji, in the years when Ameyoko was still a black market, and is now on its third generation. What is unusual about Hidemi Hosokawa is where he learned to cook: he decided to take over the family tonkatsu shop and then went and trained in French restaurants first, before coming back to the fryer. Gnavi's profile is blunt that he says little in the kitchen and simply faces one plate at a time — keeping the taste and technique he inherited from his father while folding in what he learned elsewhere. The technique is specific and old-fashioned: the frying medium is 100% lard, chosen to suit the pork they buy, and the cutlet goes in at 130°C for roughly ten minutes, then sits draining for two more, which is why the cut face comes out that faint cherry colour. The pork is domestic, from a butcher the family has used for years. His wife washes the rice for the sets by hand, picking out broken grains. The pickles come from a nuka bed inherited from the previous generation and re-fed daily. There are fourteen seats. Service is lunch only, 11:30 to 14:00, and when the day's prep is gone the shop closes, which regulars accept as the point rather than an inconvenience. Gnavi lists 「ミシュラン」 among the shop's own selling points, and there is an English menu and a German-speaking member of staff — an unexpected pairing for a fourteen-seat lunch counter in Okachimachi.
chef_bio.philosophy: Say little, prepare a lot, fry slowly, and stop when the pork runs out.
chef_bio.specialty: ヒレかつ定食 ¥2,700; ロースかつ定食 ¥2,400; 一口かつ定食 ¥1,800 (about 90 g of the same fillet, crumbed piece by piece and flashed at high heat); かきフライ from October to March using large Sanriku oysters; とんスジ煮込み ¥500, made from the sinew trimmed off during prep, in limited quantity.

anecdotes.text: The third-generation owner's route to the family fryer went through French kitchens: gnavi's profile headline is 「外国の修業もすべてはとんかつのため」 — the foreign apprenticeship was all for the sake of the tonkatsu.
Frying is 100% lard, ten minutes at 130°C, then two minutes draining — 「ほのかな桜色は丁寧な仕事の成せる技」, the faint cherry colour of the cut face being the proof of it.
The pickles come from the nuka bed handed down from the previous generation and are pickled fresh every day; the rice is washed so that no broken grains get into the sets.
Fourteen seats, entirely non-smoking, an English menu on hand, and a member of staff who speaks German.

The gnavi menu page gives current prices. Tabelog (13003593) independently confirms address, coordinates 35.708422/139.773747, phone, hours and the Monday-plus-substitute-holiday closing, with a 3.65 rating over 1,355 reviews.

gf_cross_contamination.text: One lard fryer serving every dish on the menu — pork katsu, prawn fry, oyster fry, croquette. Flour, egg and panko are the standing breading station. No dedicated fryer or wheat-free line is claimed anywhere.

soy_sauce_wheat.text: Table sauce for tonkatsu in Japan is a Worcester-style sauce built on wheat; the sets come with miso soup and pickles. No tamari or wheat-free seasoning is mentioned.

vegan_cross_contact.text: Every item is pork, prawn or oyster and the frying medium is animal fat. There is no vegetable dish on the menu beyond the shredded cabbage.

positives.text: An English menu exists and one member of staff speaks German — so a dietary question at least has a chance of being understood, even though no accommodation is published.

cultural_comfort.note: Fourteen seats, entirely non-smoking, English menu available, average spend about ¥2,500, rice and cabbage refilled once free. The catch is the window: Tuesday to Sunday, 11:30 to 14:00, closing early whenever the day's pork is gone, closed Mondays (or the Tuesday after a Monday holiday). Come at opening or accept a queue, expect to sit shoulder to shoulder, and do not plan on dinner here — there isn't one.

name: 井泉 本店
cuisine: The 1930 house that invented the katsu-sando, still trading on 「お箸できれるやわらかいとんかつ」 — tonkatsu you cut with chopsticks: rōsu set ¥1,800, hire ¥2,200, katsu-sando ¥1,100 (six pieces) or ¥1,800 (nine)
neighborhood: Yushima 3-chōme on Ueno-hirokōji — 1 min from Ueno-hirokōji (Ginza line, exit A4) and Ueno-okachimachi (Toei Ōedo, exit A4), 3 min from JR Okachimachi and from Yushima (Chiyoda line, exit 4), 4 min from Naka-okachimachi (Hibiya)
gf_detail: Wheat is the dish. Flour, egg and panko on everything fried; the katsu-sando is served in specially ordered bread; the katsu-don is cutlet finished in a soy-and-dashi broth; the croquettes, menchi-katsu and kushi-katsu share the same fryer. The site's allergen information is limited to a note about which months the omelette dishes are dine-in only. No gluten-free or wheat-free claim of any kind appears on the shop's site or on Tabelog.
vegan_detail: There is nothing animal-free on the menu: pork, prawn, crab, scallop, egg and squid shiokara, with cabbage and a cucumber salad as the only vegetables, and the salad has crab in it. The sets come with miso soup and rice.

roles: 三代目店主 (third-generation owner; the site's history page is signed 三代目店主 without a personal name)
founded 1930 by 初代 石坂一雄 (Kazuo Ishizaka)
初代女将 石坂登喜 (Toki Ishizaka), inventor of the katsu-sando
chef_bio.origin: Ueno / Shitaya, in the old Tokyo hanamachi — the shop opened there in 1930 and has kept its original bearing
chef_bio.background: 井泉 opened in Ueno in 1930 (昭和五年). The name is not a word but a signature: it was the painting pseudonym (画号) of the founder, Kazuo Ishizaka, and he intended it to be read Seisen — 「いつの間にか『イセン』の名で皆様から呼ばれる様になりました」, the shop writes, with the resignation of a house that lost an argument with its own customers a long time ago. The house line since then has been 「お箸できれるやわらかいとんかつ」 — tonkatsu tender enough to cut with chopsticks — which the third generation reads as an argument rather than a slogan: chopsticks mean Japanese, and so a tonkatsu, for all that it is yōshoku, is really washoku. The thing the shop is famous for, though, is the sandwich. Shitaya was a working hanamachi in 1930 and the geisha needed something they could eat between engagements without ruining their lipstick or their kimono. The first okami, Toki Ishizaka, had grown up unusually for a Meiji-born woman on toast and tea in the mornings, so bread was familiar to her in a way it was not to most people around her; when her husband started making tonkatsu she thought — the family's account is that she thought it 「ひょい」, offhandedly — of putting the cutlet between two slices so it could be eaten the way you eat inari-zushi or a nori roll, and had the bread specially made a size smaller so it fitted in the hand. That is, by the shop's account and by general repute, the first katsu-sando in Japan. The room was originally an 「お座敷洋食の店」, western food served on tatami, and it kept enough of the hanamachi in its bones that the film director Kawashima Yūzō took it as the model for his 1963 picture 「とんかつ一代」; the second-generation owner taught Morishige Hisaya how to fry on the set. The second generation also opened department-store counters in the late 1950s and started the shop's 暖簾分け system in the 1960s, under which cooks who trained here long enough may trade as 「○○井泉」 — each licensed branch holds a B5 board carrying the founder's calligraphy, the second generation's pig mark and a classical-Chinese permission text, and the shop notes plainly that a 井泉 without that board is not one of theirs. The dining room today still runs on the same theatre: a counter where you watch the cutlets sliced, the omelettes turned three eggs at a time, the ton-teki pan flaring and butter lobbed across the kitchen from one cook to another. Alongside tonkatsu the menu keeps a full old-Tokyo yōshoku range — prawn croquettes, crab omelette, pork sauté, hamburger, menchi, kushi-katsu with the skewers pulled out for safety — and a bentō service that will deliver locally.
chef_bio.philosophy: 「お箸＝日本人」 — a cutlet soft enough for chopsticks, because tonkatsu, western in origin, is Japanese food; kept to the founders' recipe in a room that has not been modernised out of its 1930 self.
chef_bio.specialty: かつサンド (9 pieces ¥1,800 / 6 pieces ¥1,100), the dish the shop invented; 三色サンド ¥2,000 with katsu, egg and crab-cucumber; ヒレかつ定食 ¥2,200; ロース定食 ¥1,800; ヒレかつ丼 ¥2,200.

anecdotes.text: The shop's name comes from the founder's painting pseudonym: 「昭和五年（1930年）に上野の地で、初代・石坂一雄の画号から名付けられたのが店名『井泉』の由来です。」

The katsu-sando was invented here so that the geisha of Shitaya could eat between engagements without smudging their lipstick — and the bread was specially ordered a size smaller so it would fit in the hand.

The founding okami, born in the Meiji era, was raised by forward-looking parents on toast and tea for breakfast, so bread was already part of her life when she thought to put her husband's tonkatsu between two slices 'like inari-zushi or a nori roll'.

A Tabelog diner describes the counter as an arena seat: cutlets sliced in front of you, a three-egg omelette turned by a left-handed cook, the ton-teki pan throwing flame, and a colleague lobbing butter across the kitchen on cue.

The building's Shitaya-hanamachi character caught the eye of the director Kawashima Yūzō, who used it as the model for the 1963 film 「とんかつ一代」; the shop keeps a still from the set showing the second-generation owner with Morishige Hisaya, whom he taught to fry for the part.

Cooks who train here long enough may open as 「○○井泉」 under a 暖簾分け licence, and each licensed shop holds a B5 board with the founder's calligraphy, the second generation's pig mark and a permission text in classical Chinese. The shop states flatly that a 井泉 without that board is not one of theirs.

chef_bio.japanese_sources_summary: isen-honten.jp is the shop's own site and carries the 1930 founding, the derivation of the name from the founder's 画号 and its intended reading 'Seisen', the katsu-sando origin story in the first okami's recounted words, the 暖簾分け licensing scheme and its 許可版 board, the 1963 film connection, the full priced menu, the hours 11:30–15:00 / 16:30–20:10 and the Wednesday closing (open on public holidays). Tabelog (13003619) confirms the address 文京区湯島3-40-3, coordinates 35.707479/139.772205, phone 03-3834-2901, a ¥3,000–¥3,999 band, the same hours and Wednesday closing, and a 3.52 rating over 1,891 reviews.

gf_cross_contamination.text: Flour-egg-panko breading and a shared fryer for katsu, prawn fry, prawn croquette, menchi-katsu, kushi-katsu and scallops. No dedicated equipment or wheat-free line is claimed.

soy_sauce_wheat.text: The katsu-don and the ton-teki are finished in wheat soy sauce; the table sauce is a Worcester-style wheat sauce; the sets come with miso soup. No tamari is mentioned.

vegan_cross_contact.text: Every dish contains pork, prawn, crab, scallop or egg; even the cucumber salad is a crab salad. There is no meat-free set.

cultural_comfort.note: One minute from Ueno-hirokōji station's A4 exit, open straight through from 11:30 with a short break at 15:00, closed Wednesdays but open on public holidays, and priced in the ¥1,800–¥2,800 range for a set. It is a large, busy, family-friendly room rather than a shrine — a summer children's service runs in the school holidays and there is a takeaway bentō counter. No English page on the site, but the menu is short, photographed and pointable, and a katsu-sando to take away needs no conversation at all.

enrich_note: Confirmed in Tokyo at 文京区湯島3-40-3 (Bunkyō-ku, not Taitō-ku — the light record's 「湯島 御徒町」 is the right area but the shop sits just over the ward line). Coordinates moved from the neighbourhood centroid to the Tabelog geo point, about 160 m. Founding year 1930 is from the shop's own site, not inferred. DISAMBIGUATION for whoever maintains this: 井泉 runs a 暖簾分け scheme, so a number of unrelated-in-ownership shops trade as 「○○井泉」 around Tokyo, and there is also a separate 井泉 counter inside department stores. This record is the 本店 at 湯島3-40-3 specifically; do not merge it with any other 井泉 listing.

name: ちゃんこ道場 両国駅前店
cuisine: A big, easy-going chanko izakaya one minute from Ryōgoku station: seven kinds of hotpot, banquet courses ¥4,290–¥6,600, and at lunch a ¥1,000 Fukagawa-meshi or kaisen-don with free rice refills
neighborhood: Yokoami 1-chōme, on the Kokugikan side of the station — 1 min from Ryōgoku (JR Sōbu line), 7 min from Ryōgoku (Toei Ōedo line)
gf_detail: Nothing published, and everything against it. Chanko broths in a shop like this are built on soy sauce, miso or ponzu — all wheat-carrying by default in Japan — and the pots come with tsukune and fish cake, both of which normally use a wheat binder. The rest of the izakaya menu is fried food and sashimi, and the pot is finished with rice or noodles. There is no allergen page, no gluten-free wording, and no claim of any kind on the shop's gnavi page or on Tabelog. A celiac should treat this as a no rather than an ask.
vegan_detail: The pots are chicken, pork and seafood, the broth is a meat-and-fish stock, and the house is advertised on 豊洲直送の海鮮 — seafood direct from Toyosu. The only lunch items under ¥1,000 are 深川めし (clams) and 海鮮丼 (raw fish). No vegetarian or vegan course is offered.

roles: no chef named publicly; run as a chanko izakaya rather than a stable-master's house
chef_bio.origin: Ryōgoku, Sumida-ku — the sumo quarter, opposite the Kokugikan side of the station
chef_bio.background: This is the chanko you eat in Ryōgoku when you have come for the sumo rather than for a pilgrimage: a 66-seat downtown izakaya a minute from the JR exit, open every day of the year, lunch and dinner, with orange paper-lantern lighting and no pretension at all. Its own Instagram bio claims 「創業40年」, which would put the opening in the mid-1980s, and describes it as 「本場両国のちゃんこ鍋屋」. Seven different chanko pots are offered, the flagship being the 横綱ちゃんこ at ¥2,630 a head, and the business model is really the banquet: 小結 six courses ¥4,290, 関脇 seven courses ¥5,450, 大関 eight courses ¥6,600, with two hours of free drinks bolted on for ¥2,420, and the whole room bookable for parties of 50 to 66. Lunch is the interesting part for a traveller — 深川めし, the local clam-and-rice dish of the Fukagawa fishermen, at ¥1,000 with a tuna-yamakake and an asari tsukudani on the side, or a kaisen-don at the same price, or a 両国ちゃんこ御膳 at ¥1,600, all with unlimited rice. Practically, it is one of the more accessible doors in Ryōgoku: entirely non-smoking, wheelchair-accessible, children from infants up, free Wi-Fi, power sockets, and staff who speak English and Chinese.
chef_bio.philosophy: Chanko as everyday shitamachi food rather than as an occasion — cheap at lunch, a banquet at night, open 365 days.
chef_bio.specialty: 横綱ちゃんこ ¥2,630 per person; seven chanko variants; 小結/関脇/大関 courses ¥4,290–¥6,600; lunch 深川めし and 海鮮丼 at ¥1,000; a small 'ちゃん小鍋' single-portion pot at lunch.

anecdotes.text: The shop's own Instagram bio reads 「創業40年の本場両国のちゃんこ鍋屋🍲 下町の風情溢れる店内で 絶品ちゃんこをお楽しみください。」
Fifty to sixty-six guests can take the whole room — the gnavi page pitches it for company parties and group trips, with orange lantern-shaped indirect lighting.
A recent Tabelog reviewer's summary is exactly the appeal: 「両国でちゃんこを食べる、この満足感がたまりません」 — plus the note that the room is unfussy enough to sit alone in at lunch.

chef_bio.japanese_sources_summary: The shop's gnavi page (fvjchk5z0000) carries the address 墨田区横網1-3-12, 66 seats, the lunch and dinner hours, no closing day, the ¥320 cover charge, the course prices, the ¥1,000 lunch dishes, the barrier-free and non-smoking status, and the English- and Chinese-speaking staff. Tabelog (13036713) confirms address, coordinates 35.695785/139.792947, phone 03-5624-3655, a ¥4,000–¥4,999 band and a 3.41 rating over 244 reviews, and lists online booking. The shop's Instagram supplies the 「創業40年」 claim.

gf_cross_contamination.text: A 66-seat izakaya kitchen running seven hotpots plus fried side dishes and banquet courses. No dedicated equipment, no allergen information, and the pot is finished with rice or noodles at the table.

soy_sauce_wheat.text: Chanko broths here are seasoned with soy sauce, miso or ponzu, all of which carry wheat unless a shop names a wheat-free version — and this one names nothing.

vegan_cross_contact.text: Chicken, pork and Toyosu seafood run through every pot and every course; the lunch specials are clams and raw fish.

positives.text: Staff who speak English and Chinese, plus online booking through Tabelog — so a dietary question can at least be asked in English, even though nothing is published in advance.

cultural_comfort.note: About the easiest chanko door in Ryōgoku for a visitor: one minute from the JR exit, open every day, lunch from ¥1,000, English- and Chinese-speaking staff, an entirely non-smoking room, wheelchair access, infants welcome, free Wi-Fi and power sockets, and cards, PayPay, d払い and Alipay all accepted. Two things to know before you sit: there is a ¥320 cover charge, and the room is set up for company parties, so an evening here can be loud. Lunch is calmer and much cheaper.

cuisine: A family house of chanko born in Ryōgoku in 1969 — one pot, eighteen things in it, sesame-miso or ponzu, ¥3,080 a head (fugu chanko ¥4,180); dinner only, sashimi from Toyosu alongside
neighborhood: Ryōgoku 3-chōme, east side of the station — 2 min from Ryōgoku (JR Sōbu line, east exit), 6 min from Ryōgoku (Toei Ōedo, exit A4), about 7 min by Sumida ward loop bus from Tokyo Skytree

gf_detail: The shop publishes its pot ingredient by ingredient, and the list settles it: かまぼこ (fish cake, normally bound with wheat starch), トリツミレ (chicken balls, normally bound with wheat or breadcrumb) and 油揚げ, seasoned either with a house sesame-miso or with a ponzu — ponzu is soy sauce, and soy sauce in Japan is wheat unless a shop names a gluten-free tamari. Nobody here names one. The wider menu adds 立田揚げ (starch-coated but soy-marinated), teriyaki and 酢みそ dishes. No allergen page, no gluten wording, nothing on Tabelog either.
vegan_detail: The standard pot contains swordfish, salmon, cod, scallop, prawn, hard clam, blue crab, chicken balls and pork; the fugu pot is fish throughout. The rest of the menu is sashimi, grilled fish, yakitori and duck. There is no vegetarian pot and no vegetable course.

chef_bio.chef_name: 野口雅裕 (Masahiro Noguchi) — listed as 代表者 (representative) rather than as a named chef
chef_bio.origin: Ryōgoku, Sumida-ku — the shop's own phrasing is 「両国に生まれ両国に育った」, born in Ryōgoku and raised in Ryōgoku
chef_bio.background: 友路 opened in 1969 (昭和44年) and has never left Ryōgoku, which in a sumo quarter is the whole of its claim. The pot is one recipe rather than a menu of them: eighteen ingredients — swordfish, salmon, cod, scallop, prawn, hard clam, blue crab, chicken tsukune, pork, kamaboko, abura-age, hakusai, komatsuna, harusame, tofu, negi, enoki — at ¥3,080 a head, with a choice of only two seasonings: a house sesame-miso broth, or the shop's own ponzu. A fugu version runs ¥4,180 and is eaten with the ponzu. Everything else on the card is there to be drunk with: sashimi bought daily from Toyosu and served in ¥4,400–¥6,600 platters, scallops grilled at the table, sea snail in the shell, flounder salt-grilled, and a shelf of regional sake and wine from around the country. The room is a quiet wooden one with tatami alcoves and private rooms, sumo memorabilia and wrestlers' handprints on the walls, and a crimson noren outside. The calendar is the giveaway that this is a sumo-town business: it is normally closed Sundays and holidays, but it opens right through the Ryōgoku tournaments in January, May and September, opens whenever the Kokugikan has an event on, and does not close at all in December. Daytime and Sunday service can be arranged for a group if you call ahead.
chef_bio.philosophy: One pot, done the way the house has always done it, with the region's sake beside it — 「伝統のちゃんこ、日本各地の地酒やワインでおもてなし」.
chef_bio.specialty: ちゃんこ鍋 ¥3,080 per person, eighteen ingredients, sesame-miso or ponzu; 河豚ちゃんこ鍋 ¥4,180; Toyosu sashimi platters ¥4,400–¥6,600; ほたてきじ焼き ¥990.

anecdotes.text: The shop's own description of itself: 「創業昭和44年、両国に生まれ両国に育った『友路』のちゃんこは、新鮮な肉・魚貝類・野菜を含めて18種類の具をふんだんに使ったボリューム満点の逸品。」

The opening calendar follows the sumo: closed Sundays and holidays as a rule, but open through the Ryōgoku basho in January, May and September, open for Kokugikan events, and open every day in December.

A Tabelog diner who pre-ordered the sesame-miso pot, a sashimi platter and duck in vinegared miso notes that the tatami alcove is flat rather than sunken, so you sit cross-legged, and that the room was almost entirely pairs and groups rather than solo diners.

chef_bio.japanese_sources_summary: tomoji.co.jp is the shop's own site: it gives the 1969 founding, the address 墨田区両国3-24-4, phone 03-3631-4889, fax, the representative's name 野口雅裕, the 17:00–22:30 hours and the sumo-driven closing calendar, and the full priced menu with the pot's ingredient list spelled out. Tabelog (13021577) confirms address, coordinates 35.69516/139.794126, phone, a ¥5,000–¥5,999 band, hours 17:00–22:30 (Sundays to 22:00) and a 3.27 rating over 60 reviews.

gf_cross_contamination.text: Kamaboko and chicken tsukune sit in the pot itself, and both are normally wheat-bound in Japan. The kitchen also runs 立田揚げ and other fried dishes. No wheat-free handling is claimed anywhere.

soy_sauce_wheat.text: Both of the two seasonings offered carry wheat by default: the house ponzu is a soy-sauce dressing, and the sesame-miso broth is a miso base with no type named. No gluten-free tamari or wheat-free miso is mentioned.

vegan_cross_contact.text: The standard pot is built on fish, shellfish, chicken and pork; the fugu pot is fish. The rest of the card is sashimi, grilled fish and duck.

positives.text: Unusually for a hotpot house, the shop publishes the pot's complete ingredient list on its own site, so you can see exactly what is going in before you book — which is more than most chanko restaurants offer.

cultural_comfort.note: Dinner only, Japanese only — no English page, no online booking, and the site tells you to telephone (03-3631-4889) early if you want a daytime or Sunday sitting. It is a quiet, mostly-reserved wooden room where parties of two and up eat a pot together, so a solo walk-in will feel conspicuous; call ahead and name your pot and seasoning. Tatami alcoves are flat, not sunken, so you sit cross-legged on the floor. Bear the calendar in mind: closed Sundays and holidays except during the January, May and September sumo tournaments, Kokugikan event days, and the whole of December.

enrich_note: Confirmed in Tokyo at 墨田区両国3-24-4; coordinates moved from the neighbourhood centroid to the Tabelog geo point (about 130 m). Everything above except the coordinates and the rating comes from the shop's own site. The light record's gf 'ask' has been downgraded to 'no' on the strength of the published ingredient list (kamaboko, tsukune) and the two soy/miso seasonings.

name: 石臼挽き手打 蕎楽亭
address_ja: 〒162-0825 東京都新宿区神楽坂3-6 神楽坂館1F
cuisine: A thirty-seat Kagurazaka counter that mills its own Aizu buckwheat on volcanic-rock stones — 二色そば ¥1,050 puts a 10%-binder noodle beside a jūwari one in the same basket, and the tempura (¥2,400) is live prawn and live conger fried in front of you
neighborhood: Kagurazaka 3-chōme, near the foot of the slope — 4 min from Iidabashi (Yūrakuchō / Namboku lines, exit B3), 5 min from JR Iidabashi west exit, 5 min from Ushigome-Kagurazaka (Toei Ōedo), 7 min from Kagurazaka (Tōzai line)
hours_raw: [火〜土] 11:30〜14:00／17:00〜20:00　定休日：日曜・月曜・祝日（食べログ、2026年時点）　※公式サイト（2020年アーカイブ）は「昼 11:30〜15:00／夜 17:00〜21:00、日・月・祝休」と記載　※その他臨時休業有り
gf_detail: This is a case where the shop's own ingredient page rules it out more firmly than a soba shop usually can be ruled out. Kyourakutei mills wheat on the premises: 「うどん・ひやむぎ」 are made from Ibaraki, Saitama and Gunma wheat, 「店内の小麦専用石臼で自家製粉」 — self-milled in the shop on a dedicated wheat stone mill. Airborne wheat flour is a standing condition of the room. The seasoning is worse for a celiac than usual too: the house shōyu is either a three-year Shōdoshima soy sauce or an Aichi 白醤油, and white soy sauce is made predominantly from wheat rather than soy. The jūwari half of the nishoku is not a way round this — it is boiled and served in the same kitchen and dipped in the same wheat tsuyu. Add a tempura station frying to order. No gluten-free claim exists; none could honestly be made.
vegan_detail: The dashi is published and it is entirely animal: 尾札部産の真昆布 with 枕崎産の本節 (Makurazaki katsuobushi), イリコ (dried sardine) and 乾椎茸. So the tsuyu, the tempura dipping sauce and the soup dishes all carry bonito and sardine. Eggs come from a named Sagamihara farm and are used in the kitchen. Konbu and shiitake are in the stock, but never on their own.

roles: also runs 天ぷら蕎楽亭, the shop's one-party-a-day tempura offshoot in Yochōmachi
chef_bio.origin: Kagurazaka, Shinjuku-ku; the buckwheat comes from Yanaizu in the Aizu district of Fukushima
chef_bio.background: Kyourakutei is a soba shop that decided to be a mill. Kenji Hasegawa buys unhulled buckwheat — 玄そば — mainly from Yanaizu-machi in the Aizu district of Fukushima, and grinds it himself inside the shop on stones cut from Aizu volcanic rock, the weight of the stone determining what kind of noodle can be made from it; he grinds both the whole grain and the hulled 丸ぬき. The signature order, 二色そば at ¥1,050, exists to show the difference: one basket, two noodles, a 一割つなぎ (10 % binder) beside a jūwari, so you taste the same grain milled and cut two ways. That is the same instinct applied to everything else on the ingredient list, which the shop publishes item by item: dashi from Ozatsube ma-konbu with Makurazaki hon-bushi, iriko and dried shiitake; soy sauce either three-year-aged from Shōdoshima or white shōyu from Aichi; wasabi from Yugashima in Izu; Senju negi; spicy daikon from Aizu; a house kombu salt they call 「神楽坂の塩」; eggs from the Inoue poultry farm in Sagamihara. The counter is a single slab of timber, and the tempura fried across it uses live prawns and a live conger eel, served with the house salt or a ten-tsuyu — one of the reasons the room reads more like a kappō than a noodle shop despite the ¥1,050 headline price. Thirty seats, ten of them at the counter, entirely non-smoking. Tabelog has it in its そばEAST百名店 2025 list at 3.75 over 1,909 reviews, and its Michelin appearance is a standing part of the shop's own publicity. Hasegawa also runs a separate 天ぷら蕎楽亭 at 新宿区余丁町1-14, reservation-only, one party a day, a single ¥15,000 omakase; that shop has been on and off hiatus. His greeting page is characteristically plain: that he is able to go on cutting soba today is because of the people who come, and that although he knows he often falls short, he hopes they will keep raising the shop.
chef_bio.philosophy: Mill it yourself and let the grain answer for itself — hence two noodles from the same buckwheat in one basket, and an ingredient list published down to the salt.
chef_bio.specialty: 二色そば ¥1,050 (jūwari beside a 10 %-binder noodle, both stone-milled in the shop); tempura of live prawn and live conger ¥2,400 with the house kombu salt; 牛すじ煮込み ¥760; self-milled udon and hiyamugi in season.

anecdotes.text: The buckwheat is milled in the shop on stones of Aizu volcanic rock, and the shop keeps a second, separate stone mill used only for wheat — 「店内の小麦専用石臼で自家製粉しております」.
The ingredient page runs to the salt: 「神楽坂の塩（自家製の昆布塩）」, a kombu salt the shop makes itself and names after the street.

The tempura is fried from live stock — two live prawns and a live conger — and Hasegawa's second business, 天ぷら蕎楽亭 in Yochōmachi, takes one party a day by reservation only for a single ¥15,000 omakase.
The counter is cut from a single board of timber; the whole room is thirty seats, ten at that counter, and entirely non-smoking.

chef_bio.japanese_sources_summary: The shop's own site at kyourakutei.com now serves an empty Adobe Portfolio shell; the substantive pages survive in the Internet Archive, and the 2020 capture read here carries the owner's signed greeting (店主 長谷川健二), the complete 素材 list (Aizu-Yanaizu buckwheat self-milled in-shop; wheat from Ibaraki/Saitama/Gunma self-milled on a dedicated wheat stone mill; dashi of ma-konbu, hon-bushi, iriko and dried shiitake; Shōdoshima three-year or Aichi white soy sauce; Izu wasabi; Senju negi; Aizu spicy daikon; house kombu salt; Sagamihara eggs), the address 新宿区神楽坂3-6 神楽坂館1F, phone 03-3269-3233, hours and Sunday/Monday/holiday closing, and the sister shop 天ぷら蕎楽亭 at 新宿区余丁町1-14. HotPepper adds the 30-seat/10-counter layout, the volcanic-rock millstone, the ¥1,050 二色そば, the ¥2,400 live-prawn-and-conger tempura and the ¥760 beef-sinew stew. Tabelog (13000479) confirms the name 石臼挽き手打 蕎楽亭, the address and coordinates 35.700785/139.739516, the phone number, a ¥4,000–¥4,999 dinner band, current hours of 11:30–14:00 and 17:00–20:00 with Sunday, Monday and holiday closing, そばEAST百名店 2025 selection and a 3.75 rating over 1,909 reviews.

gf_cross_contamination.text: Wheat is milled inside the shop. The published ingredient list states that the udon and hiyamugi are made from Ibaraki, Saitama and Gunma wheat self-milled on a dedicated wheat stone mill on the premises — so wheat flour is being ground in the same room as everything else.
A tempura station fries to order across the counter, and the same kitchen boils both soba and udon.

soy_sauce_wheat.text: The house soy sauce is either a three-year-aged Shōdoshima shōyu or an Aichi 白醤油. White soy sauce is brewed predominantly from wheat, so this is more wheat than an ordinary koikuchi, not less.
The jūwari half of the 二色そば offers no way round it: it is served with the same wheat tsuyu, from the same kitchen.

vegan_cross_contact.text: The dashi is published and animal: ma-konbu with Makurazaki hon-bushi, iriko (dried sardine) and dried shiitake. Every tsuyu and soup in the shop carries it.

positives.text: The shop publishes its whole ingredient list, down to the salt and the egg farm — so what is in the food can be checked before you go, which is exactly what makes the gluten verdict here so clear-cut.

cultural_comfort.note: Thirty seats, ten at the counter, non-smoking, no reservations for the ordinary service and no English published. HotPepper's listing says cards, e-money and QR payment are all unavailable, so bring cash. Lunch is 11:30 and there will be a queue — it is a Tabelog Hyakumeiten shop in a busy part of Kagurazaka. Closed Sundays, Mondays and public holidays, and it takes irregular days off besides, so telephone (03-3269-3233) if the trip matters. Sitting at the counter and watching the tempura is the point; ordering the 二色そば needs three syllables of Japanese and nothing more.

enrich_note: Confirmed in Tokyo at 新宿区神楽坂3-6 神楽坂館1F; coordinates moved from the neighbourhood centroid to the Tabelog geo point (about 550 m — the light record's pin was materially wrong). The light record's gf 'ask' and vegan 'limited' are both downgraded — 'ask' is not defensible for a shop that mills wheat on site and seasons with white soy sauce, and 'limited' is not defensible against a published bonito-and-sardine dashi.

name: かんだやぶそば
address_ja: 〒101-0063 東京都千代田区神田淡路町2-10
cuisine: Tokyo's most theatrical old soba house, founded 1880 and rebuilt around its garden in 2014 — せいろうそば ¥1,320 under a sing-song order-call, or a full kaiseki course upstairs at ¥12,100–¥14,300
neighborhood: Kanda-Awajichō 2-chōme, in the old Renjaku-chō quarter behind Yasukuni-dōri — 3 min from Awajichō (Marunouchi line, exit A3) or Kanda (Ginza line), 6 min from JR Kanda or Akihabara
hours_raw: 11:30〜ラストオーダー20:00　定休日：水曜日（祝祭日の場合は変更あり）
gf_detail: The shop rules it out in writing, on its own site, in one sentence: 「ビーガン・ベジタリアン・グルテンフリーに関しましては、主力料理の性質上対応いたしかねますので予めご了承ください」 — owing to the nature of our main dishes we are unable to accommodate vegan, vegetarian or gluten-free requests. Everything downstream agrees: 釜揚げうどん and 小田巻蒸し are wheat noodles, the tempura and かき揚げ are wheat batter, the soba-zushi is rolled around simmered kanpyō and egg, and the tsuyu is a strong Edo wheat shōyu. This is a clear published refusal, not an absence of information — treat it as final.
vegan_detail: Refused in the same published sentence as gluten-free. Even without it: the tsuyu is a bonito dashi, the かまぼこ, 鴨ロース, あいやき, あなご and 玉子焼き are all animal, and the two kaiseki courses are built around duck, conger and prawn. The 刺身湯葉 (¥1,650) and わさびいも (¥1,320) are the only plant dishes on the card, and both are served with soy sauce.

chef_bio.origin: Kanda-Awajichō, Chiyoda-ku — the Renjaku-chō block where the shop has traded since 1880
chef_bio.background: かんだやぶそば has been on the same Kanda corner since 1880, and its owner's greeting counts the years out loud: the shop is in its 144th year, and in the tenth since it reopened. The style descends from the late Edo yabu line, and the two things everyone remembers about the room are not on the plate. One is the noren-to-table ritual: 「いらっしゃい——」 called and answered around the room, and each order sung back to the kitchen in a stretched, chanted cadence — 「せいろう〜そば〜、あいやき〜」 — so that even the name of the dish is archaic (せいろう, not せいろ). The other is the garden. The building sits behind its own hedge of bamboo — the 藪 of the name — and the ground-floor seats look into green rather than onto the street; the fifth-generation owner, Kōtarō Hotta, writes that the intention in rebuilding was to make a shop that belonged to the town and to share the garden's green with the neighbourhood. The reopening he is counting from is October 2014, an entire rebuild; a Tabelog reviewer setting out the shop's history records that it lost its building to the Kantō earthquake, then to the war, and then to a fire in the Heisei era, and that each time the noren went back up. The rebuild took the chance to make an old shop unusually accessible: level floors, an accessible lavatory, and a lift to the first floor. Downstairs seats 77 across tables and a small raised alcove; upstairs is twenty seats in three private rooms for six, six and eight, where the two kaiseki courses are served — 団子坂 at ¥12,100 and 連雀 at ¥14,300, each running 先付け, 椀物, そばがき, a grilled course of duck or white-grilled conger, chawanmushi, prawn 'raft' tempura, seiro soba and a soba manjū. The everyday card is the classical Edo repertoire at Edo prices for a landmark: せいろうそば ¥1,320, 天ぷらそば ¥2,860, 鴨せいろう ¥3,190, plus the drinking dishes a soba shop is judged on — 焼きのり served over its own charcoal box, 板わさ, 鴨ロース, 天抜き and 鴨抜き (the tempura or duck course with the noodles taken out and served as a soup).
chef_bio.philosophy: 「美味しいおそばを気持ち良く」 — good soba, pleasantly — the line the fifth generation says has not changed since the founding, alongside a deliberate effort to keep the rebuilt shop part of its street rather than above it.
chef_bio.specialty: せいろうそば ¥1,320; あいやき ¥2,200 (duck breast with negi cooked in duck fat); 天抜き / 鴨抜き ¥2,200 (the topping without the noodles, as a soup); 小田巻蒸し ¥2,420, a chawanmushi with udon, conger, ginkgo, prawn and duck in it; kaiseki courses 団子坂 ¥12,100 and 連雀 ¥14,300.

anecdotes.text: Orders are chanted back to the kitchen in a stretched, sung cadence — a Tabelog reviewer writes that it is 「注文というより、詠唱に近い」, closer to an incantation than an order, and that asking why the shop says せいろう rather than せいろ would itself be vulgar: the word is part of the tradition.
The fifth-generation owner's greeting page counts the shop into its 144th year and its tenth since the October 2014 rebuild, and is signed 「かんだやぶそば 五代目 堀田康太郎」.
The 2014 rebuild made a Meiji-era soba house barrier-free: level floors throughout, an accessible lavatory, and a lift to the first-floor private rooms.

The house takes reservations only for the ground floor and for courses upstairs; walk-ins take a numbered ticket from a tablet at the door, and at New Year the ticket machine is switched off entirely and everyone simply queues.

chef_bio.japanese_sources_summary: yabusoba.net is the shop's own site. Its 店舗案内 page carries the address 〒101-0063 千代田区神田淡路町2-10, phone 03-3251-0287, hours 11:30 to a 20:00 last order, Wednesday closing, the October 2014 whole-building reopening, the seat counts (1F 77 seats, 2F 20 seats in three private rooms) and the barrier-free provisions — and, critically for this dataset, the flat statement that vegan, vegetarian and gluten-free cannot be accommodated. The ご挨拶 page is signed by the fifth-generation owner and dates the shop to its 144th year. The お品書き page gives the full priced menu and both kaiseki courses. Tabelog (13000334) confirms address, coordinates 35.697009/139.768694, phone, a ¥1,000–¥1,999 band, Wednesday closing, 11:30–20:30 daily otherwise, and a 3.50 rating over 2,751 reviews, and its long-form reviews supply the order-chanting and the fire/earthquake/war rebuilding history.

gf_cross_contamination.text: The shop states outright that it cannot accommodate gluten-free requests because of the nature of its main dishes. Wheat udon (釜揚げうどん, 小田巻蒸し) and a tempura station run alongside the soba in the same kitchen.

soy_sauce_wheat.text: The tsuyu is a strong Edo wheat shōyu and no tamari is offered; the two plant dishes on the card — 刺身湯葉 and わさびいも — are themselves eaten with soy sauce.

vegan_cross_contact.text: Vegan and vegetarian requests are declined in the same published sentence as gluten-free. The tsuyu is a bonito dashi and both kaiseki courses are built on duck, conger and prawn.

staff_allergy_handling.text: The only published position on dietary requests is a refusal — 「主力料理の性質上対応いたしかねますので予めご了承ください」. That is honest and it is also final; do not send a celiac here to negotiate at the door.

cultural_comfort.note: Physically one of the most accessible historic restaurants in Tokyo: step-free floors, an accessible lavatory and a lift to the private rooms upstairs, all built into the 2014 rebuild. There is an English page on the site, the ordering system at the door is a tablet that issues a number, and the menu is short. Expect a queue at weekends — reviewers describe it as having become a sightseeing stop — and expect the room to be loud with the staff's called-and-answered greetings, which is the house style rather than a lapse. Ground-floor tables and upstairs courses can be reserved through the site; the walk-in queue cannot.

enrich_note: Confirmed in Tokyo at 千代田区神田淡路町2-10; coordinates moved from the neighbourhood centroid to the shop's own Google Maps point, which matches Tabelog's (about 570 m — the light record's pin was materially wrong). The gf and vegan verdicts here are not inferences: the shop publishes an explicit refusal of vegan, vegetarian and gluten-free requests on its 店舗案内 page, so the light record's gf 'ask' / vegan 'limited' are both corrected to 'no'. The shop's own menu includes 釜揚げうどん — wheat udon — and a seasonal ひやむぎ, both boiled in the same kitchen as the soba, and the tempura for the ¥2,310 天ぷらそば is fried on site in wheat batter. chef_bio.background: 神田まつや was founded in 1884 (明治17年) by Ichizō Fukushima. Two generations on, after the Great Kantō Earthquake, the shop passed to Masakichi Odaka, and the Odaka family has run it since. The lineage of the noodle itself is traceable in a way that is unusual even among Tokyo soba houses: the second-generation Odaka, Kenjirō, learned his technique from Sakutarō Sekiya, who had come out of the Gyoranzaka Yabu-soba and later founded the Ōmori Umeyashiki Yabu-soba; the third, Toshi, learned at the 蕎風会, the trade circle, alongside the previous masters of Kanda Yabu Soba, Ueno Rengyokuan and Kanda-Nishikichō Sarashina, and the shop's own account calls the present 神田まつや the sum of that schooling. Machine-made noodles were abandoned for entirely hand-cut ones in 1963. The tsuyu is deliberately on the strong side — 「下町のなごりとも云える少し濃い目」 — and the house argues that the whole art is the balance of that dark dip against a plain noodle: 「手打ちそばと汁だけなのに、なぜこれほど美味しいのか、不思議です」. The room is the point as much as the food. It has around sixty seats, a wooden interior kept deliberately in its founding character, an old kneading bowl and a pillar clock on the wall, and the shop notes that the quiet hour is between 15:00 and 17:00. Its most famous regular was the novelist Shōtarō Ikenami, who lived nearby and came in geta. Prices have barely moved into the present century — a mori is ¥770 — and the shop also sells raw soba in three- and six-portion packs to take home, and runs a page about the buckwheat fields in Sakai, Ibaraki and in Hokkaidō that it visited in 2007 to see where its flour comes from.
chef_bio.philosophy: The Edo dip and the hand-cut noodle, unchanged: strong, dark tsuyu on the shitamachi side, a room kept in its founding character, and prices that let people eat here every week.
chef_bio.specialty: もりそば ¥770; ごまそば ¥935, the shop's own recommendation and, it says, a surprise to first-timers; かけそば ¥770; 天ぷらそば ¥2,310 with two large kuruma prawns, mitsuba and yuzu; 鴨南ばん, かしわ南ばん, 鴨せいろ, 釜揚げうどん, 焼き鳥 and わさびかまぼこ as the drinking dishes.

anecdotes.text: The novelist Shōtarō Ikenami, famous as a gourmand, was a regular and walked here in geta; the shop says the old kneading bowl and pillar clock on the wall still bring those days back.
The switch from machine-made noodles to entirely hand-cut ones happened in 1963: 「因みに機械製麺を全部『手打ち』に切り替えたのは昭和38年のことでした。」

The second-generation Odaka learned his noodle technique from Sakutarō Sekiya of the Gyoranzaka Yabu-soba line; the third learned alongside the previous masters of Kanda Yabu Soba, Ueno Rengyokuan and Kanda-Nishikichō Sarashina in the 蕎風会 circle.
About sixty seats, always busy — the shop's own advice is that the quiet window is between three and five in the afternoon.
In autumn 2007 the shop went to look at its own supply, visiting buckwheat fields in Sakai, Ibaraki and in Hokkaidō and the stone mills that grind for it.

Tabelog (13000340) lists the shop as 神田まつや 本店 and confirms address, coordinates 35.696123/139.768797, phone, a ¥1,000–¥1,999 band, Sunday and Monday closing with slightly later last orders than the site states, and a 3.66 rating over 3,165 reviews.

gf_cross_contamination.text: Wheat udon (釜揚げうどん) and a seasonal ひやむぎ are on the shop's own menu and come out of the same kitchen as the soba; the tempura is fried in wheat batter on site. No wheat-free handling is claimed.

The soba's binder ratio is not published. Hand-cut Edo soba is conventionally 20 % wheat, and nothing on the site suggests otherwise — do not read 手打ち as jūwari, and do not read jūwari as gluten-free in any case.

soy_sauce_wheat.text: The house is explicit that its tsuyu is a strong, dark shitamachi one, which means wheat soy sauce; it is presented as half the reason to come. No tamari is mentioned.

vegan_cross_contact.text: The shop's own copy stresses that the tsuyu is carried by a firm dashi, and its recommended dishes are duck, chicken, yakitori and kamaboko. No animal-free preparation exists.

cultural_comfort.note: An old, packed, communal room where you will be seated with strangers at a shared table and expected to eat and go. No English page on the site, no reservations, no online booking; the menu is short and pointable but the drinking dishes are not translated. Closed Sundays and Mondays — a common trip-wrecker, since the neighbouring Kanda Yabu Soba closes Wednesdays instead. Aim for the shop's own recommended quiet window, 15:00 to 17:00, if you would rather not queue. Prices are low enough (¥770 for a mori) that this is one of the cheapest historic meals in central Tokyo.

gf_detail: Kabayaki is soy-sauce lacquer: the tare a shop like this has been topping up for a century is soy sauce, mirin and sugar, and soy sauce in Japan is wheat unless a shop names a gluten-free tamari. Kubota names none, and publishes no allergen information at all. The rest of the card is no better — the 柳川なべ, 親子丼, 玉子丼 and 鶏の照焼丼 are all soy-seasoned, and the sets come with soup and pickles. The one item worth knowing about is the 白焼 set at ¥5,200: eel grilled plain, without tare. It is the least-wheat thing in the building, but it comes to the table with soy sauce and wasabi, it is cooked over the same charcoal and by the same hands as the kabayaki, and no wheat-free handling is claimed — so it is a lead to ask about, not a safe order.

roles: 四代目 (fourth-generation owner; writes the shop's 四代目ブログ)
chef_bio.origin: Sotokanda, Chiyoda-ku — the family firm 有限会社久保田商店 has traded on this block since 1897
chef_bio.background: うなぎ久保田 was founded in 1897 (明治30年) and is on its fourth generation, Taizō Kubota, who writes the shop's blog. The building is the surprise. In 1973 the family asked Mayumi Miyawaki — the architect known for houses, and one of the more provocative figures in post-war Japanese domestic architecture — to extend the existing shop, and what he produced is a boldly coloured exterior meant to evoke the Pacific, the eel's spawning ground; it is not what anyone expects to walk into on a Kanda backstreet looking for a hundred-year-old eel restaurant. Across the road the shop keeps its 卸部の立場, a wholesale holding station where eel, loach and carp swim in water pumped up from an underground well until they are needed. There is a second, stranger thread in the family: Hiroji Kubota, the Magnum Photos photographer, is the younger brother of the third-generation owner Shōichirō and therefore the fourth generation's uncle — his photo books are kept on the ground floor and his prints hang on the third, so a meal here comes with a small, unadvertised Magnum exhibition. The house seats about a hundred over several floors, all non-smoking with a small smoking room, and there is no lift, only stairs. The everyday draw is the una-don: ¥1,800, Monday to Saturday from eleven, made with the shop's top-grade eel, and gone when it is gone. Above it the ladder is conventional and steep — unajū sets ¥4,200 / ¥5,200 / ¥6,800, a 特製中入れ丼 at ¥9,000, kabayaki and shirayaki sets, and cheaper non-eel sets (親子丼 ¥1,800, 玉子丼 ¥1,600, 柳川なべ ¥3,000) that let a table eat at different prices. The shop also runs a sake club, a gift and mail-order business, and takeaway.
chef_bio.philosophy: Not stated as a slogan; the shop's own emphases are the well water its live stock is held in, the century of continuity, and the building it commissioned rather than inherited.
chef_bio.specialty: うな丼 ¥1,800, weekday lunch only and until sold out, made with the same top-grade eel as the expensive sets; うな重定食 ¥4,200 / 上 ¥5,200 / 特上 ¥6,800; 白焼定食 ¥5,200; 柳川なべ定食 ¥3,000 (loach); 特製中入れ丼（重）定食 ¥9,000.

anecdotes.text: The current building is a 1973 extension designed by the architect Mayumi Miyawaki, and the shop explains its bold exterior colours as an image of the Pacific Ocean — the eel's spawning ground.
Across the street the shop keeps its wholesale 立場, with eel, loach and carp swimming in water pumped from an underground well.
Hiroji Kubota of Magnum Photos is the younger brother of the third-generation owner and the fourth generation's uncle; his books are on the first floor and his prints hang on the third.
A Tabelog regular's summary of what to order beyond the rice box: 「肝焼きを特製の山椒で」 — the liver skewers with the house sanshō, which is a vivid green and strongly scented, and a cup of sake.

chef_bio.japanese_sources_summary: unagi-kubota.jp is the shop's own site. Its 店舗情報 page gives the 1897 founding, the address 〒101-0021 千代田区外神田5-6-9, phone 03-3831-6082, the split lunch and dinner service with its unusually explicit last-entry and 'we put the fire out at' times, Sunday and public-holiday closing plus seasonal and ad-hoc closures, about 100 seats, all non-smoking with a small smoking area, no lift, no car park, and the note that cards are accepted except during the ¥1,800 una-don service and peak days such as Doyō no Ushi. The same page carries the Miyawaki commission, the well-water holding tank and the Hiroji Kubota connection. The お品書 page gives the full priced menu. Tabelog (13016711) confirms the name うなぎ 久保田, address, coordinates 35.703666/139.772983, phone, hours 11:00–15:00 and 17:00–21:00, Sunday and holiday closing, 銀座線末広町駅2番出口徒歩2分, and a 3.61 rating over 497 reviews.

gf_cross_contamination.text: A single charcoal grill and one tare pot serve the whole room; the shirayaki is cooked on the same bars as the kabayaki. No dedicated equipment or wheat-free line is claimed anywhere on the site.

soy_sauce_wheat.text: Kabayaki tare is a soy-sauce glaze, and the 柳川なべ, 親子丼, 玉子丼 and 鶏の照焼丼 are all soy-seasoned. No gluten-free tamari is named.

vegan_cross_contact.text: Eel, loach, carp, chicken and egg; live stock held in tanks across the street. No plant-based dish exists on the menu.

positives.text: A published 白焼定食 at ¥5,200 — eel grilled without tare — means there is at least one dish in the building that is not lacquered in soy sauce, and it is on the printed menu rather than a special request. That makes it a sensible thing to ask about; it does not make it verified safe.

cultural_comfort.note: No English page and no lift — the building is stairs only, which matters if steps are a problem. The service windows are tight and unusually precisely stated: last entry around 14:10 for lunch and 19:10 for dinner, with the fire put out at 14:30 and 20:00, so arriving at ten to closing will not work. Closed Sundays and public holidays, plus New Year, Golden Week and a summer break. Cards are accepted except during the cheap ¥1,800 una-don service and on peak days like Doyō no Ushi, so carry cash if you are coming for the bargain. Around a hundred seats means you can usually get in outside the eel-eating festivals.

roles: no individual chef named; the shop credits 「暦40年以上のうなぎ職人」, eel craftsmen of forty years and more
one of four shops in the きくかわ group (神田, 第一ホテル東京, 上野毛, 御殿場)
chef_bio.origin: Kanda-Sudachō, Chiyoda-ku — the shop opened on this spot in 1947 and has not moved
chef_bio.background: 神田きくかわ opened in 1947, in the food shortages right after the war, on the straightforward proposition that people needed something to put stamina back into them; it has been on the same Kanda-Sudachō corner for over seventy-five years. Its signature is a rule about proportion rather than a recipe: the eel is laid across the box so that no rice shows through — 「ご飯が見えないぐらいにうなぎで覆います」 — a practice the shop says it has kept since it opened, so that a customer leaves thinking they really did eat eel today. The method is Edo-style and slow. The eel is split from the back rather than the belly, since Edo disliked the association with seppuku; it is white-grilled, then steamed, then painted with tare and grilled again, roughly forty minutes per order, which is why the shop prints something close to an apology-that-is-not-one on its own page: 「江戸前のうなぎ料理は、時間がかかる。せかされると、はんぱな仕事になるんでね。でもかならずいい仕事するから、まかせなよ。」 Two technical details it is proud of: the skewers are not bamboo but custom-made metal ones, bundled piano wire, chosen because metal carries the heat inward and finishes the flesh from inside as well as out; and the live eels are rested for one to three days before use in a 立て場 at the group's Kaminoge branch, a site the family chose for its good groundwater near the Tōmei expressway's Tokyo interchange, so that the fish spit out mud and firm up — the Kanda, Hibiya and Kaminoge shops all draw from that holding tank. The Kanda room seats 68 over two floors, including tatami, entirely non-smoking, with a 28-seat table area upstairs; average spend is around ¥7,000. Takeaway unajū and pre-ordered 折詰弁当 with tare and sanshō are a substantial part of the business.
chef_bio.philosophy: Cover the rice completely, split from the back, take the forty minutes it takes, and do not be hurried.
chef_bio.specialty: うな重 in graded sizes (a 2026 diner records the 【イ】, a whole-and-a-half eel, at ¥5,450); 折詰弁当 with tare and sanshō to take away; pre-ordered kabayaki or shirayaki for home.

anecdotes.text: The house rule since 1947: 「お重の中身は、ご飯が見えないぐらいにうなぎで覆います」 — the box is covered so completely that no rice shows, so that you leave thinking 「今日は思いっきりうなぎを食べたなあ」.
Not bamboo skewers but custom metal ones made from bundled piano wire, because the metal conducts heat into the flesh and cooks it from the inside as well.

Live eels are rested one to three days in a holding station at the group's Kaminoge branch — a site chosen for its groundwater, near the Tōmei expressway's Tokyo interchange — before being sent to the Kanda, Hibiya and Kaminoge shops.

The shop's own printed line to customers in a hurry: 「勝手言ってもうし訳ないけど、江戸前のうなぎ料理は、時間がかかる。せかされると、はんぱな仕事になるんでね。でもかならずいい仕事するから、まかせなよ。でがけに一声かけてもらえりゃ大変助かります。」 — ring ahead as you set out and it helps a great deal.

chef_bio.japanese_sources_summary: The shop's gnavi pages (g116702) carry the 1947 founding and its post-war motive, the rice-covered-completely rule, the back-splitting / shirayaki / steam / tare / re-grill sequence at about forty minutes, the piano-wire skewers, the Kaminoge holding tanks and groundwater, the address 〒101-0041 千代田区神田須田町1-24-2, hours 11:00–21:00 weekdays and 11:00–20:30 at weekends and holidays, Monday closing with a Tuesday substitute, 68 seats including tatami, fully non-smoking, an average spend of ¥7,000 (¥6,500 at lunch), a full range of cards, and the sister shops 第一ホテル東京店, 上野毛店 and 御殿場店. Tabelog (13000339) confirms name, address, coordinates 35.694429/139.770822, phone 03-3251-1506, a ¥6,000–¥7,999 band, the same hours and closing, and a 3.56 rating over 1,168 reviews, and carries a 2026 review pricing the うな重【イ】(一尾半) at ¥5,450. The company's own site (kanda-kikukawa.co.jp) exists but its shop and menu pages render only through JavaScript and returned no readable content.

gf_cross_contamination.text: One charcoal grill, one tare pot, one specialism. Even the 白焼き is grilled on the same bars as the tare-painted eel. No dedicated equipment or wheat-free procedure is claimed.

soy_sauce_wheat.text: The final two stages of the shop's own described method are applying tare and grilling again. Tare is soy sauce, mirin and sugar; no gluten-free tamari is named.

vegan_cross_contact.text: An eel-only kitchen. Nothing on the menu is plant-based.

positives.text: Kabayaki or shirayaki can be pre-ordered for takeaway, which at least means an un-lacquered eel is something the kitchen already makes to order — a starting point for a conversation, not an assurance.

cultural_comfort.note: One of the more visitor-ready old shops in Kanda: gnavi publishes English, Korean and both Chinese versions of the listing, the room is 68 seats over two floors and entirely non-smoking, all the major cards are taken, and it sits at the mouth of the Ginza line's exit 5. Two things to plan for. First, time — the eel is cooked from raw when you order it, about forty minutes, and the shop's own advice is to telephone as you set out. Second, price: expect around ¥7,000 a head, ¥6,500 at lunch. Reservations are taken for takeaway only; for a table you turn up. Closed Mondays, or the following Tuesday when the Monday is a public holiday.

enrich_note: Confirmed in Tokyo at 千代田区神田須田町1-24-2; coordinates moved from the neighbourhood centroid to the Tabelog geo point (about 300 m). CATEGORY FLAG: filed as MOM_AND_POP, but きくかわ is a four-shop group — 神田店 plus 第一ホテル東京店, 上野毛店 and 御殿場店, sharing a central eel-holding station at Kaminoge. Family-scale, but not a single independent shop; the merge script may want to reclassify. The light record's cuisine string mentioned 「白焼き・炭火焼」: charcoal is right, but 白焼き at this shop is a stage in the cooking of every eel rather than a headline dish, and that distinction matters for anyone reading the record for gluten reasons. menu_url is left null because the company's own menu page renders only via JavaScript and returned no content.

name: 神田食堂 本店

gf_detail: Nothing published and nothing workable. The entire menu is simmered in miso or soy — motsu in a 「秘伝の味噌」, saba in a sweet miso glaze, chicken and daikon in a soy-dashi broth — and Japanese soy sauce is wheat by default while the miso type is not stated (barley miso would be gluten too). The 60-second promise also tells you something operationally: dishes are held ready and plated fast, which is not a service model that pauses to build a special plate.
vegan_detail: Every dish on the standing menu is animal: offal, beef tendon, chicken and daikon, mackerel, pork miso soup, and a mapo tofu that in a Japanese teishoku shop is made with minced pork. The seasonal items are cold pork shabu and chicken breast with summer vegetables. The only meat-free things on the board are the ¥150 side dishes and the rice.

roles: operated by 株式会社神田食堂 (formerly 株式会社インベスターズ); 代表取締役 磯大輝 (Daiki Iso)
chef_bio.origin: Uchi-Kanda, Chiyoda-ku — a 2020s Kanda operator rather than an inherited shop
chef_bio.background: 神田食堂 is a new business wearing old clothes, and it is worth being clear about that because the light record filed it as a mom-and-pop 老舗. The operating company, 株式会社神田食堂, was incorporated on 17 January 2023 (renamed from 株式会社インベスターズ) under 磯大輝, and runs five restaurants: the Kanda honten, a 馬喰町店 in Nihonbashi-Yokoyamachō, a 新御徒町店 announced for a 1 September opening, plus an オリオン餃子 franchise in Tsukuba and 東の餃子 in Utsunomiya. What it does, it does with real focus. The concept is one sentence — 「うまい定食を、60秒で。」 — a nikomi teishoku specialist that puts all its labour into prep so that service can be instant: 「仕込みに時間をかけ、段取りを磨き、提供は最速で。早いのに、うまい。」 The copy is unusually candid about the reasoning, which is that a定食 is the meal that has to fit into a limited lunch break or the twenty minutes after work, and that respecting that time is the job. The board is short and cheap: motsu-nikomi ¥1,000, beef tendon ¥1,300, chicken-and-daikon ¥1,000, saba in miso ¥1,200, tonjiru ¥700, mapo tofu ¥1,000, with rice upgrades at ¥100–200 and a ¥300 discount for taking the dish without the set. It is open every day, 11:00 to 16:00 and 17:00 to 22:00, and it delivers through Uber Eats. Tabelog reviewers describe a clean, bright room with a long central table that makes it easy to eat alone, and staff who seat you immediately.
chef_bio.philosophy: 「うまい定食を、60秒で。」 — put the hours into the prep so the customer's minute is not spent waiting.
chef_bio.specialty: もつ煮込み定食 ¥1,000 (the recommended dish, offal carefully cleaned and simmered in a house miso); 牛すじ煮込み定食 ¥1,300; さばの味噌煮定食 ¥1,200; 豚汁定食 ¥700; 鶏大根定食 ¥1,000; seasonal 冷しゃぶと鬼おろしポン酢定食 ¥1,100.

anecdotes.text: The concept page states the promise and immediately hedges it: 「神田食堂は、手仕込みの煮込み定食を、できたてのまま60秒で提供する定食屋です」 … 「※混雑状況によって提供時間が遅れる場合があります。」
The company's own reasoning for the speed: 「定食は、人生に寄り添うごはんだと私たちは思っています。忙しい朝に、限られた昼休みに、仕事終わりの数十分に……」
A Tabelog diner looking for a motsu-nikomi set found one here, and notes the long central table means a solo customer can sit as if at a counter.
Ordering the dish without the rice-and-soup set knocks ¥300 off the price — useful if you are eating twice in an afternoon.

chef_bio.japanese_sources_summary: kandashokudo.com is the operator's own site: the 店舗案内 page gives the honten address 〒101-0047 千代田区内神田一丁目18番11号, the 11:00–16:00 / 17:00–22:00 hours, 年中無休, and the walking times from JR Kanda west exit and from Kanda, Awajichō and Ogawamachi stations, together with the 馬喰町店, the planned 新御徒町店 and the two gyōza businesses. The 運営会社 page gives the company name (旧：株式会社インベスターズ), the 17 January 2023 incorporation, the representative director 磯大輝 and 「飲食事業(飲食店5店舗運営)」. The concept page carries the 60-second promise verbatim. Tabelog (13310236) confirms the address including the building and floor, coordinates 35.691905/139.767165, phone 070-9367-3205, a ¥1,000–¥1,999 band, the hours and 年中無休, describes it as 「並ばず、待たず、手作り。煮込み定食専門店」, and carries the full current priced menu; it has a 3.35 rating over 66 reviews.

gf_cross_contamination.text: A fast-turnover teishoku kitchen with no published allergen information and a service model built on plating pre-made stews in under a minute — not a setup that stops to prepare a separate plate.

soy_sauce_wheat.text: Every main is simmered in miso or soy: motsu in a house miso, saba in a miso glaze, chicken and daikon in a soy-dashi broth, and every set comes with miso soup. The miso type is not stated, so barley miso cannot be ruled out either.

vegan_cross_contact.text: Offal, beef tendon, chicken, mackerel, pork and a pork-based mapo tofu. Nothing on the standing board is meat-free apart from the ¥150 side dishes.

cultural_comfort.note: About as low-friction as Tokyo eating gets: bright and clean, open every day from 11:00 to 22:00 with a break at 16:00, a long communal table that makes a solo lunch unremarkable, a short board of six or seven dishes at ¥700–¥1,300, free rice sizing and reservations available through Tabelog. No English is published, but the menu is short, photographed and pointable, and there is an Uber Eats listing if you would rather eat elsewhere. The one thing to reset is expectation: this is a good-value modern canteen, not an old Kanda institution.

No gluten-free option, no allergen information, and a nine-seat counter with one pot has nowhere to put a separate order even if it wanted to. Not a candidate.
vegan_detail: A pork-and-soy broth with chāshū as the standard topping; the shop's own signature bowl is built on it. The only listed toppings are chāshū, nori, naruto (fish cake) and spinach. Nothing animal-free is offered.

roles: Tokyo branch of the Nagaoka, Niigata original; run day to day by a master and one member of staff
chef_bio.origin: Nagaoka, Niigata — the parent shop; this branch opened in Akihabara in 2009
chef_bio.background: 青島食堂 is one of the very few regional ramen styles to have made a serious dent in Tokyo without becoming a chain about it. The parent shop is in Nagaoka in Niigata — gnavi describes it as an old-established shop dating from the Shōwa era — and 生姜醤油ラーメン, ginger-soy ramen, is Nagaoka's local style: a dark soy broth with pork behind it and enough grated ginger to change the whole shape of the bowl, poured over a thin, soft, curly noodle. The Akihabara branch opened in 2009, five or six minutes' walk from the station on the Shōwa-dōri side, and it has been queueing ever since; gnavi's own listing warns of about an hour's wait at lunch, and Tabelog reviewers describe a line outside and then a second line of benches inside for six more people. The scale is deliberately small: nine counter seats, and, per gnavi's account, a master and one female member of staff running the whole thing. The bowls stay under ¥1,000 — the Tabelog price band is 〜￥999 — which for a shop with 3,660 reviews and a 3.74 rating puts it among the best-value famous bowls in central Tokyo. The named orders are 青島ラーメン (the house bowl), 長岡ラーメン and 青島チャーシュー, with chāshū, nori, naruto and spinach as the toppings you choose between. Service is 11:00 to 17:00 only, closed Tuesdays, and the shop will close early if it runs out.
chef_bio.philosophy: One regional bowl, done as it is done at home in Nagaoka, cheap, from nine seats.
chef_bio.specialty: 青島ラーメン — ginger-forward shōyu over a thin curly noodle; 長岡ラーメン; 青島チャーシュー. All under ¥1,000.

anecdotes.text: Gnavi's summary: an hour's wait at lunch, opened in Akihabara in 2009, parent shop in Nagaoka since the Shōwa era, and the whole place run by the master and one member of staff across nine counter seats.

A Tabelog diner arriving at 14:00 in blazing heat found five people already queueing and five more behind them within a minute, and describes a second waiting bench for six inside the door once you get that far.
A gnavi reviewer's one-line version of the appeal: 「生姜の香りがする醤油ラーメンです。チャーシューも柔らかくて美味しいんです。麺もシコシコしててて美味しい。」

gf_cross_contamination.text: One pot, one noodle basket, nine seats. Wheat noodles are the dish; there is no separate anything.

soy_sauce_wheat.text: The style is defined by its tare: 生姜醤油, ginger and soy sauce. No gluten-free tamari is named and no allergen information is published.

vegan_cross_contact.text: Pork broth with chāshū standard; the alternative toppings are nori, naruto (fish cake) and spinach.

cultural_comfort.note: Nothing to negotiate — you queue, you sit at one of nine counter seats, you order a bowl under ¥1,000, you eat and you leave. Budget the queue rather than the meal: gnavi warns of about an hour at lunch and reviewers confirm it, so go at opening (11:00) or late in the afternoon, remembering that service stops at 17:00, that Tuesday is the closing day, and that the shop may shut early if it sells out. No English is published, but 「青島ラーメン」 is the only phrase you need.
